\section[deprimido]{deprimido — depressed, low}

\label{lesson:ES-C717-deprimido}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for disappointed, then the Spanish for disappointment.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: deprimido}
\textbf{deprimido} — \textquotedblleft{}depressed, low\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Desde que perdió el trabajo está deprimido.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{Since he lost his job he has been depressed.}
\end{quote}

Used with \emph{estar}. For the illness, say \emph{tener depresión}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{deprimido} is the participle of \emph{deprimir}, which comes from Latin \emph{dēprimere} \textquotedblleft{}to press down\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB), a learned word built on \emph{premere} \textquotedblleft{}to press\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{deprimido}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{deprimido}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{deprimido}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for disappointed, then the Spanish for disappointment, then say \emph{deprimido} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does deprimido mean? (\textquotedblleft{}Depressed, low\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[desahogarse]{desahogarse — to let off steam, to pour one's heart out}

\label{lesson:ES-C717-desahogarse}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for disappointment, then the Spanish for depressed.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: desahogarse}
\textbf{desahogarse} — \textquotedblleft{}to let off steam, to pour one's heart out\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Necesito hablar contigo para desahogarme.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{I need to talk to you to get it off my chest.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Desahogarse con alguien} — to open up to someone. \emph{El desahogo} is the relief it brings.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{desahogarse} is built on \emph{ahogar} \textquotedblleft{}to choke, to drown\textquotedblright{} with the prefix \emph{des-}: to stop choking. \emph{Ahogar} comes from spoken Latin \emph{affōcāre}, Latin \emph{offōcāre} \textquotedblleft{}to choke\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB), from \emph{faucēs} \textquotedblleft{}throat\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{desahogarse}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{desahogarse}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{desahogarse}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for disappointment, then the Spanish for depressed, then say \emph{desahogarse} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does desahogarse mean? (\textquotedblleft{}To let off steam, to pour one's heart out\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.

\section[el sufrimiento]{el sufrimiento — suffering}

\label{lesson:ES-C717-sufrimiento}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for depressed, then the Spanish for to let off steam.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: el sufrimiento}
\textbf{el sufrimiento} — \textquotedblleft{}suffering\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
La guerra causa mucho sufrimiento.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{War causes a lot of suffering.}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{sufrimiento} is built on \emph{sufrir} with the ending \emph{-miento}; \emph{sufrir} is usually traced to Latin \emph{sufferre} \textquotedblleft{}to bear up under\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[la lágrima]{la lágrima — the tear (from the eye)}

\label{lesson:ES-C717-lagrima}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for to let off steam, then the Spanish for suffering.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: la lágrima}
\textbf{la lágrima} — \textquotedblleft{}the tear (from the eye)\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Tenía lágrimas en los ojos.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{She had tears in her eyes.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Llorar a lágrima viva} — to cry your eyes out.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{lágrima} comes from Old Spanish \emph{lagrima} (EtymDB), from Latin \emph{lacrima} \textquotedblleft{}tear\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.

\section[desesperado]{desesperado — desperate}

\label{lesson:ES-C717-desesperado}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for suffering, then the Spanish for the tear.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: desesperado}
\textbf{desesperado} — \textquotedblleft{}desperate\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Estaba desesperado por encontrar piso.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{He was desperate to find a flat.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Estar desesperado por} + infinitive.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{desesperado} is built on \emph{desesperar} \textquotedblleft{}to despair\textquotedblright{}, which EtymDB traces to Latin \emph{dēspērāre} \textquotedblleft{}to lose hope\textquotedblright{}, from \emph{spērāre} \textquotedblleft{}to hope\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}
